title: Effects of Medium-to-Inoculum Ratio and Metabolic Supplementation on Bacterial Cellulose Production by the Kombucha Symbiotic Community
content: Bacterial cellulose (BC), produced by SCOBY (symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeast) consortia in kombucha, is a low-cost, sustainable biomaterial, but its yield is highly sensitive to fermentation conditions. This study investigated how fresh tea medium-to-SCOBY inoculum ratio and supplementation with α-ketoglutaric acid (α-KG), citric acid, magnesium sulfate, and glycerol affect BC biofilm formation, medium pH, and total polyphenol content over 14 days of static fermentation. A higher medium-to-inoculum ratio (2:1) yielded significantly more wet and BC biomass than a lower ratio (1:2), and this ratio was selected as the baseline conditions for further experiments. Both α-KG and citric acid, tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates, showed biphasic, dose-dependent effects on BC yield: moderate supplementation (0.25 g/L α-KG; 0.5 g/L citric acid) approximately doubled biofilm mass relative to control, while higher doses markedly suppressed or abolished BC growth, with α-KG showing stronger inhibition at high concentration than citric acid. α-KG supplementation also modestly reduced total polyphenol content in kombucha in a dose-dependent manner. In contrast, MgSO₄ (0.8 g/L) and glycerol (40 g/L) both significantly decreased BC yield relative to the control, and glycerol also reduced polyphenol content. Medium pH declined over cultivation in all groups regardless of treatment, indicating that supplementation affected cellulose biosynthesis rather than the overall acidification dynamics of fermentation. These findings identify α-KG and citric acid, at defined moderate concentrations, as promising low-cost supplements for enhancing BC yield in kombucha-based systems.
